scenes.tts: In middle-aged and elderly organ donors, much of the healthy oesophageal lining carried a mutation in one cancer gene, notch one. How does one mutant cell's family come to fill a lining that is replaced all the time?
scenes.narration: In middle-aged and elderly organ donors, much of the healthy oesophageal lining carried a mutation in one cancer gene, NOTCH1. How does one mutant cell's family come to fill a lining that is replaced all the time?
scenes.caption: In middle-aged and elderly organ donors, much of the healthy oesophageal lining carried a mutation in one cancer gene, NOTCH1. How does one mutant cell's family come to fill a lining that is replaced all the time?
scenes.visual: Open on a top-down view of a sheet of lining: a honeycomb of about 200 small BLUE hexagons filling the frame, gently shimmering. While the first sentence plays, irregular GOLD patches grow outward from a few seed hexagons until they cover a large share of the sheet (draw several patches of different sizes; label in the corner 'schematic'). Label at top left: 'human donors'. Label beside the largest patch: 'NOTCH1-mutant: est. 12 to 80%'. Small source line under it: 'Martincorena et al., 2018'. On 'How does one mutant cell's family', the question appears across the top in white: 'How does one family fill it?'.
Title 'Fate, Not Speed' fades in over the top of the sheet for 2 s while the gold patches keep a faint shimmer. The question text from the hook fades out under it.

scenes.tts: Experiments in mouse oesophagus show how. Here is the lining, cut across. Only the bottom row of cells divides. That row is the basal layer, and its dividing cells are progenitors.
scenes.narration: Experiments in mouse oesophagus show how. Here is the lining, cut across. Only the bottom row of cells divides. That row is the basal layer, and its dividing cells are progenitors.
scenes.caption: Experiments in mouse oesophagus show how. Here is the lining, cut across. Only the bottom row of cells divides. That row is the basal layer, and its dividing cells are progenitors.
scenes.visual: The honeycomb tilts away and rotates into the side view, becoming THE WORLD for the whole film: left two-thirds of the frame, a cross-section of oesophageal lining filling about 70% of frame height. A thin GREY horizontal line near the bottom is the basement membrane. On it sits one row of twelve round BLUE cells (progenitors), each with a small white clock face whose hand turns at a steady rate. Above the row, four or five layers of GREEN cells (differentiating) that get flatter the higher they are and drift slowly upward like an escalator; at the top edge the flattest green cells peel off and float out of frame. Right third: a panel for tiles and labels. GOLD marks the mutant clone throughout. Labels 28 pt or larger, at most 5 words, full opacity. Something always moves: the escalator drift and the clock hands never stop. The gold patches fade to blue as it turns, so the new view starts all blue and green. Label top left morphs from 'human donors' to 'mouse oesophagus'. Show first, then name: the bottom row of blue cells pulses once as the narrator says 'bottom row', then the label 'basal layer' slides in beside the row. On 'progenitors', one blue cell in the middle of the row divides (pinches into two blue circles that shuffle sideways to make room) and the label 'progenitor' appears with a line to it.

scenes.tts: Each daughter of a progenitor either stays in the bottom row or leaves it. Cells that leave differentiate, ride upward and are shed from the top. So the lining keeps its cell number steady only if, on average, it makes as many cells as it loses.
scenes.narration: Each daughter of a progenitor either stays in the bottom row or leaves it. Cells that leave differentiate, ride upward and are shed from the top. So the lining keeps its cell number steady only if, on average, it makes as many cells as it loses.
scenes.caption: Each daughter of a progenitor either stays in the bottom row or leaves it. Cells that leave differentiate, ride upward and are shed from the top. So the lining keeps its cell number steady only if, on average, it makes as many cells as it loses.
scenes.visual: Follow one division in the bottom row: one daughter stays in the row (stays BLUE), the other is squeezed up out of the row, turns GREEN and begins to flatten. Track it with a soft highlight as it rides the escalator up through the green layers over about 8 s and peels off the top edge. Label 'differentiating' follows it upward for the first few seconds. On 'as many cells as it sheds', two small counters appear in the right panel: 'made' (BLUE) and 'shed' (GREEN), ticking up together at the same rate while divisions at the bottom and peeling at the top keep going.

scenes.tts: Watch one progenitor divide. Each division has three possible outcomes. Both daughters stay: call that P P. One stays and one leaves: P D. Or both leave: D D.
scenes.narration: Watch one progenitor divide. Each division has three possible outcomes. Both daughters stay: call that PP. One stays and one leaves: PD. Or both leave: DD.
scenes.caption: Watch one progenitor divide. Each division has three possible outcomes. Both daughters stay: call that PP. One stays and one leaves: PD. Or both leave: DD.
scenes.visual: The counters slide away. In the right panel, three tiles build one at a time, each a tiny animation of one division seen in the same side view: tile 1, a blue cell splits into two blue cells that both stay on the line, labelled 'PP'; tile 2, one blue stays and one turns green and lifts off, labelled 'PD'; tile 3, both daughters turn green and lift off, labelled 'DD'. Each tile builds as the narrator names it. Meanwhile, in the main view, divisions of all three kinds keep happening along the bottom row.

scenes.tts: In normal lining, these outcomes are balanced. P P comes up as often as D D. So on average, each division leaves one progenitor behind. One in, one out, and the bottom row holds steady.
scenes.narration: In normal lining, these outcomes are balanced. PP comes up as often as DD. So on average, each division leaves one progenitor behind. One in, one out, and the bottom row holds steady.
scenes.caption: In normal lining, these outcomes are balanced. PP comes up as often as DD. So on average, each division leaves one progenitor behind. One in, one out, and the bottom row holds steady.
scenes.visual: Under the three tiles, a tally labelled 'progenitors left behind' (no numbers spoken; schematic). Each time a division happens in the main view, its tile flashes and a small marker drops into the tally: two blue dots for PP, one for PD, none for DD. PP and DD flash equally often. A level line on the tally hovers at one dot per division and the label 'one in, one out' appears beside it on that phrase. The bottom row stays exactly twelve cells wide throughout.

scenes.tts: Now one basal cell loses notch one, and we mark it gold. Every cell descended from it inherits the gold mark. That family of cells is a clone.
scenes.narration: Now one basal cell loses Notch1, and we mark it gold. Every cell descended from it inherits the gold mark. That family of cells is a clone.
scenes.caption: Now one basal cell loses Notch1, and we mark it gold. Every cell descended from it inherits the gold mark. That family of cells is a clone.
scenes.visual: The tally fades. In the middle of the bottom row, one blue cell turns GOLD with a soft flash; label 'Notch1 lost' points to it. It divides: one gold daughter stays in the row, the other turns pale green with a GOLD rim (differentiating but still marked) and rides upward. On 'That family of cells is a clone', a dashed GOLD outline wraps around the gold cell and its marked descendants and the label 'clone' appears.

scenes.tts: Its clock runs no faster than its blue neighbours' clocks. The mouse data point to one difference. Its divisions give P P a little more often than D D.
scenes.narration: Its clock runs no faster than its blue neighbours' clocks. The mouse data point to one difference. Its divisions give PP a little more often than DD.
scenes.caption: Its clock runs no faster than its blue neighbours' clocks. The mouse data point to one difference. Its divisions give PP a little more often than DD.
scenes.visual: Zoom gently on the gold cell and its two blue neighbours: three clock faces side by side, each hand turning at a steady pace; the gold hand is never ahead of the blue ones, but the hands are not drawn locked together. Label 'no faster' beside the gold clock. On 'one difference', the three tiles return in the right panel, now with GOLD borders, and the PP tile grows slightly larger while the DD tile shrinks slightly (schematic; no numbers). The clock hands keep turning.

scenes.tts: Before we run the clock forward, a question. On average, will the gold clone hold steady, die out, or spread along the row?
scenes.narration: Before we run the clock forward, a question. On average, will the gold clone hold steady, die out, or spread along the row?
scenes.caption: Before we run the clock forward, a question. On average, will the gold clone hold steady, die out, or spread along the row?
scenes.visual: Zoom back out to the whole cross-section. The question card appears in the right panel in white: 'Hold steady, die out, or spread?'. The gold cell sits in the bottom row; the escalator keeps drifting and the clocks keep turning.
Hold the question card on screen. Near-silence. Only slow ambient motion: escalator drift and turning clock hands. No division of the gold cell during the pause.

scenes.tts: On average, it spreads. In this simplest picture, each division leaves a little more than one progenitor on average. Round after round, that small tilt compounds. Now watch the edges. Blue neighbours there differentiate and lift away.
scenes.narration: On average, it spreads. In this simplest picture, each division leaves a little more than one progenitor on average. Round after round, that small tilt compounds. Now watch the edges. Blue neighbours there differentiate and lift away.
scenes.caption: On average, it spreads. In this simplest picture, each division leaves a little more than one progenitor on average. Round after round, that small tilt compounds. Now watch the edges. Blue neighbours there differentiate and lift away.
scenes.visual: Fast-forward: a small label 'time' with a moving arrow appears top right, and every clock hand speeds up as time runs forward; the gold clock is never ahead of its neighbours'. On 'simplest picture', a small corner tag reads 'simplest picture'. The gold patch in the bottom row widens from one cell to two, four, then about seven cells, while marked gold-rimmed green cells stream upward above it. Label 'schematic' in the corner. On 'watch the edges', highlight the blue cell at each edge of the gold patch: it turns green and lifts up into the escalator, and a gold daughter slides sideways into the gap.

scenes.tts: Each progenitor the gold clone keeps takes room a neighbour gives up. So the clone won by keeping more of its daughters as progenitors. Fate, not speed.
scenes.narration: Each progenitor the gold clone keeps takes room a neighbour gives up. So the clone won by keeping more of its daughters as progenitors. Fate, not speed.
scenes.caption: Each progenitor the gold clone keeps takes room a neighbour gives up. So the clone won by keeping more of its daughters as progenitors. Fate, not speed.
scenes.visual: Repeat the edge event once more on the other side, slower: a blue neighbour lifts off, the gap opens, a gold cell fills it; label 'room given up' with an arrow to the gap. On 'keeping more of its daughters', the gold PP tile in the right panel pulses. On 'Fate, not speed', those words appear under the tiles in GOLD. The gold clock keeps its 'no faster' label; its hand is never ahead of its neighbours'.

scenes.tts: Now look down on the lining from above. With time, gold patches spread among the blue. The lining changed because which cells are there changed. On average, the gold cells divided no faster.
scenes.narration: Now look down on the lining from above. With time, gold patches spread among the blue. The lining changed because which cells are there changed. On average, the gold cells divided no faster.
scenes.caption: Now look down on the lining from above. With time, gold patches spread among the blue. The lining changed because which cells are there changed. On average, the gold cells divided no faster.
scenes.visual: The side view tilts back into the top-down honeycomb from the hook (the same sheet, now labelled 'mouse oesophagus', 'schematic' in the corner). Several gold seeds appear in different places; most grow into irregular patches over a few seconds and one small seed winks out. Clock faces are shown faintly on a few hexagons, gold ones never ahead of blue ones. On 'which cells are there changed', the patchwork pulses once.

scenes.tts: Is a lining full of these clones dangerous? And how could anyone tell fate from speed in a living tissue? The text below picks up there.
scenes.narration: Is a lining full of these clones dangerous? And how could anyone tell fate from speed in a living tissue? The text below picks up there.
scenes.caption: Is a lining full of these clones dangerous? And how could anyone tell fate from speed in a living tissue? The text below picks up there.
scenes.visual: The patchwork shrinks to the left half. In the right half, two question lines appear in white, one per question: 'Dangerous?' and 'Fate or speed: how to tell?'. A small down arrow labelled 'in the text' appears under them. Gold patches keep a faint shimmer.
End card: the line below in white on the dark ground, with a small gold patch beside it.
scenes.line: In this lining, a clone spreads by fate, not by speed.
